The I Ching, the Classic of Changes, is one of the oldest books of China. At its heart are 64 figures called hexagrams, each made of six lines, whole or broken, counted from the bottom up.
Each hexagram is two trigrams of three lines, one above the other. The eight trigrams are Heaven, Lake, Fire, Thunder, Wind, Water, Mountain and Earth.

Each hexagram has a judgment on the figure as a whole, a short text for each of its six lines, and an image drawn from its two trigrams. The hexagrams are in the book’s own order, traditionally credited to King Wen.
Hold a question in mind, or write it down. An open question works better than a yes or no one. No question is fine too.

Each line is cast with three coins: heads count three, tails two, so the total is 6, 7, 8 or 9. Seven is a whole line and eight a broken one. Nine is a whole line and six a broken one that are both about to change: these are the changing lines.
Cast the lines from the bottom up, one press each, or all at once. The phone tosses the coins with a secure random source.
The older method, counting out yarrow stalks, has slightly different odds: whole lines change more often than broken ones. Turn on Yarrow-stalk odds in Settings to cast with them.
Start with the judgment and the image of the hexagram you cast. They speak to the situation as a whole.
If any lines are changing, read the texts for those lines. They are marked beside the figure: a circle on a whole line, a cross on a broken one.
The changing lines turn into their opposites and make a second hexagram. Its judgment suggests where things are heading. With no changing lines, the first hexagram is the whole answer.
Hexagrams 1 and 2 have a seventh text, for when all six lines change. It is shown when that happens.
The translation is James Legge’s, published in 1882 in The Sacred Books of the East, volume 16. It is in the public domain and is given here as he wrote it.

Legge puts words in parentheses to carry the sense of the terse Chinese. His spelling of the Chinese names is an old one, Khien for Qián, Khwan for Kūn; the characters and the pinyin are shown beside them.
The short English names of the hexagrams are written for this app.
The Book of Changes: cast a hexagram with three coins or yarrow-stalk odds, read it in James Legge’s translation, and keep a journal of your readings.

Everything you put in this app stays on this phone. It has no internet access, so nothing is sent anywhere, and nothing is collected about you. There are no ads, no analytics and no tracking.
